extracted.intended_audience: schoolboys and learners of English (and their teachers); elementary/secondary students studying prescriptive English grammar
extracted.subtask_description: Prescriptive elementary English grammar rules and usage guidance intended to teach boys how to speak and write correctly; covers parts of speech, inflectional rules, agreement, formation of words, and common errors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition and purpose of Grammar
rubrics_metrics.description: GRAMMAR is the art of speaking and writing any language with propriety; English grammar teaches to speak and write the English language properly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Grammar explains universal principles common to all languages and gives the rules needed to speak and write with propriety. Intended as foundational guidance for pupils once earlier lessons are mastered.

rubrics_metrics.name: Parts of speech (overview)
rubrics_metrics.description: Classification and roles of the parts of speech (nouns, pronouns, adjectives, verbs, adverbs, prepositions, conjunctions, interjections, articles, participles).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Each part of speech is defined, exemplified, and rules for formation and use are given in later sections (see individual entries).

rubrics_metrics.name: Tenses — Imperfect, Perfect, Pluperfect (forms & examples)
rubrics_metrics.description: Forms and examples of imperfect, perfect, and pluperfect tenses (e.g., 'I couldst send', 'They have eaten', 'We might have had').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples illustrate conjugation and auxiliary usage across persons (I, thou, he, we, ye, they) including archaic second-person forms (thou couldst, thou shouldst).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use and distinction of shall and will
rubrics_metrics.description: Shall and will both denote future time but differ in signification: 'shall' in first person foretels; 'will' in first person intimates resolution/promises; in second and third persons 'shall' often expresses commands/promises and 'will' simply foretels.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'I shall dine at home.' (foretell) vs 'I will reward the good.' (resolution/promise). Guidance on when each auxiliary implies promise, command, or mere future.

rubrics_metrics.name: Modal verbs: may/can/might/could/would/should/must/ought
rubrics_metrics.description: Modal verbs may, can, might, could, would, should, must, ought indicate ability, permission, supposition, obligation, inclination, or hypothetical situations, with tense/meaning distinctions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: May/can relate to present and future ('I can (now) write; if he come (to-morrow) you may speak to him'). Might/could often imply an impediment. Should = obligation; would = inclination. When 'have' follows (should have, could have) they relate to past. Use and contrasts are exemplified.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of do/did (periphrastic do)
rubrics_metrics.description: Do and did are used to mark the action itself or time with greater force and to avoid repetition; they may also supply the place of another verb to prevent unnecessary repetition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'I do applaud thee; I did love him.' They also substitute for repeated verbs in subsequent phrases ('you do not learn so fast as she does').

rubrics_metrics.name: Subject–verb agreement (general)
rubrics_metrics.description: The verb must agree with its subject in number and person; many examples of incorrect agreement are given (e.g., 'John and James was first at school' is wrong).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guidance and many contrasting examples show correct vs incorrect agreement; teaching warns against treating plural subjects as singular, and gives many anti-pattern examples.

rubrics_metrics.name: Agreement with compound subjects and proximity rule
rubrics_metrics.description: When the neuter verb stands between a singular and plural noun or pronoun, it agrees best with that immediately before it; compound subjects joined by and are usually plural.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'He and you are to blame' (plural). For mixed constructions (singular + plural joined by or/nor) the verb commonly agrees with the nearer subject. The text also gives counterexamples and common mistakes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Verb agreement after collective and mass nouns
rubrics_metrics.description: Collective nouns and certain constructions may be treated as singular or plural depending on sense (examples: 'The army is at hand' vs plural uses).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples show contexts where nation/parliament/army are treated as singular or plural depending on whether the body is considered as a unit or as individuals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of articles — indefinite (a/an) and definite (the)
rubrics_metrics.description: A and an are indefinite (do not point out particular person/thing); the is definite (points out a particular person/thing).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rules: 'A' used before 'few' and 'many' even with plural substantives ('a few apples'); proper and abstract nouns generally have no article except by eminence or distinction; 'the' sometimes used before adverbs in comparative/superlative constructions ('the oftener I read...'). Examples clarify use and exceptions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Nouns — primitive, derivative, simple, compound (definitions)
rubrics_metrics.description: Primitive word: comes from no other; derivative: comes from another; simple: not compounded; compound: made up of two or more words.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: king, raven (primitive); kingdom, ravenous (derivative); sea, earth (simple); sea-fish, land-tortoise (compound).

rubrics_metrics.name: Formation of plurals (regular rules)
rubrics_metrics.description: Substantives ending in s, x, ch, sh form plurals by adding -es; endings in ce/ge/se/ze add s and form another syllable; nouns ending in y preceded by a consonant change y to -ies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rules illustrated with examples (fox → foxes; church → churches; boy → boys).

rubrics_metrics.name: Formation of plurals (f/fe → ves and doubling rules)
rubrics_metrics.description: Substantives ending in f or fe often form plural by changing f/fe to -ves (calf → calves; knife → knives), with listed exceptions (chief, cliff, proof, roof, etc.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exceptions enumerated so pupils can memorize irregular patterns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Irregular plurals and foreign plurals
rubrics_metrics.description: Many nouns form irregular plurals (child → children; foot → feet; mouse → mice) and words from foreign languages generally retain original plurals (erratum → errata; phenomenon → phenomena).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lists of common irregulars and foreign plural forms provided as guidance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Nouns with no plural or no singular
rubrics_metrics.description: Certain nouns have no plural (e.g., bread, butter) and others have no singular (e.g., bellows, scissors); some have both numbers alike (deer, sheep).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guidance and examples to help pupils recognize uncountable and pluralia tantum nouns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cases of nouns (nominative, genitive, dative, accusative, vocative, ablative)
rubrics_metrics.description: Definitions: Nominative names the thing; Genitive implies possession (often with 'of' or 's); Dative expresses to/for; Accusative is the object; Vocative calls/invokes; Ablative expresses from/derived from.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: How to recognise each case (ask who/which/what for nominative; 'of' for genitive; to/for for dative), and examples showing apostrophe use, plural possesives, and when apostrophe may be omitted.

rubrics_metrics.name: Gender of nouns and formation of feminine forms
rubrics_metrics.description: Lists masculine/feminine pairs and formation methods: adding another substantive (man-servant, hen-sparrow), changing termination (actor → actress), adding -ess, -rix, etc.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Extensive lists of examples and patterns (e.g., abbot → abbess; administrator → administratrix) to teach formation of feminine nouns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pronouns — types and agreement (possessive, relative, demonstrative, definitive, attributive)
rubrics_metrics.description: Pronouns classified (possessive, relative, demonstrative, definitive, attributive); relative pronouns must have antecedents; possessive forms (mine/thine) used before vowels; reflexive/self forms explained.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rules on pronoun agreement (person, number, case), antecedent reference, and correct pronoun case in isolation (answers to questions must use the nominative form). Examples and cautions about incorrect uses ('Thou and me are both accused').

rubrics_metrics.name: Pronoun case errors and correct ordering
rubrics_metrics.description: Pronoun case must be correct in subject/object positions; order and pairing conventions (you and I, he and you) and correct nominative/accusative forms are emphasized.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Many incorrect examples ('I and him are culpable', 'Him and she eat heartily') contrasted with correct forms; guidance to prefer 'you and I' as subjects and 'him and me' as objects when appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adjectives — comparison and formation
rubrics_metrics.description: One-syllable adjectives (and many two-syllable) form comparative by -er and superlative by -est; longer adjectives use more/most. Some form superlatives with -most (uppermost) or are irregular (chief, extreme).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rules for spelling changes when adding endings (final -e, doubling consonants), and warnings that adjectives are sometimes improperly used as adverbs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Verbs — person/number endings and conjugation patterns
rubrics_metrics.description: Second person singular present/imperfect formed by adding -st/-est; third person formed by adding -th/-eth/-s; plural persons share first person singular endings; regular verbs conjugated like 'to learn'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Spelling rules when adding endings (verbs ending in -e add 'r' or 'th'; doubling consonants for monosyllables ending in single consonant with single vowel). Examples and irregular verb notes given.

rubrics_metrics.name: Regular vs irregular verbs and defective verbs
rubrics_metrics.description: Regular verbs differ from irregulars in the imperfect tense and passive participle formation; defective verbs lack many tenses/persons and must be joined to infinitives of other verbs (e.g., 'ought to learn').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Defective verbs (e.g., ought) require another verb's infinitive; irregular verbs' irregularities are to be memorized; all regular verbs conjugate like 'learn'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Formation and use of participles (active and passive)
rubrics_metrics.description: Active participle becomes adjective (a loving father); passive participle forms passive voice; formation rules include preserving silent e (singing vs singeing) and doubling consonants in certain cases (commit → committing).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Active participles with 'the' and 'of' can become substantives; participles can replace infinitives elegantly; examples and orthographic rules provided.

rubrics_metrics.name: Passive and progressive constructions
rubrics_metrics.description: Active participle with auxiliary 'to be' forms progressive (I am learning); passive is formed with passive participle joined to 'to be' (I am loved).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples show formation across tenses: Present 'I am loved', Imperfect 'I was loved', Perfect 'I have been loved'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Subjunctive mode formation
rubrics_metrics.description: The subjunctive is formed by adding a conjunction to the indicative and dropping personal terminations in the 2nd/3rd persons singular of the present, and in the 2nd singular of other tenses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Brief note on formation and use; examples illustrate subjunctive constructions in hypothetical situations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adverbs — recognition, formation, placement, and comparison
rubrics_metrics.description: Adverbs answer how/how much/when/where; can be formed from substantives, adjectives, participles, or prepositions (man → manfully; sweet → sweetly; loving → lovingly; near → nearly).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adverb placement generally near the verb; comparative and superlative forms exist (often, oftener, oftenest); irregular comparisons (much/more/most). Warning: two negatives destroy one another (double negatives are affirmative).

rubrics_metrics.name: Prepositions — recognition and use
rubrics_metrics.description: A preposition can be recognized by following it with a substantive/pronoun to see if it makes sense (from London to York; above them).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prepositions usually precede their objects and should be placed before the pronoun they govern ('to whom will you give that pen'); many prepositions can become adverbs in different senses; different relations require different prepositions (convey with, on, in, etc.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Conjunctions — classes and their functions
rubrics_metrics.description: Principal conjunctions arranged into classes: Copulative (and, also), Disjunctive (or, nor), Concessive (though, although), Causal (for, because), Conditional (if, unless), Rational (therefore), Adversative (yet, nevertheless), Exceptive (but, except), Suspensive (whether...or).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Some conjunctions correspond with others in sentence construction (though ... yet). Examples and pairings provided to teach correct connective use.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interjections — types and examples
rubrics_metrics.description: Interjections express emotions or calls and are classified (joy, grief, wonder, praise, aversion, surprise, attention, silence, exultation, calling).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples provided for each class (joy: 'ha!'; grief: 'ah! alas!'; attention: 'hark!'). Nouns may be used as interjections (O shame!).

rubrics_metrics.name: Ellipsis — omission for brevity and avoidance of repetition
rubrics_metrics.description: Ellipsis is omission of a word necessary to grammatical construction to avoid repetition and express ideas in fewer words.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Principal design is to avoid repetition; many examples show how words are omitted but sense retained ('I love and fear him' = I love (him) and I fear (him)). Advises attention to elliptical constructions in compound sentences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sentence definitions: simple and compound
rubrics_metrics.description: A sentence is a number of words joined to make a complete sense. A simple sentence has at least one noun and one verb; a compound sentence joins two or more simple sentences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'John reads' (simple). 'Charles reads, and William writes' (compound).

rubrics_metrics.name: Identification and correction of inelegant/false constructions (common errors)
rubrics_metrics.description: A list of common incorrect or inelegant constructions (e.g., 'Gooses is very silly birds', 'John and I reads better than you', 'Thou and me is both accused') to be avoided.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provides many erroneous examples and the correct forms implicitly by contrast throughout the text; pupils are warned to learn correct agreement, case, and idiom.

rubrics_metrics.name: Orthographic and spelling guidance in inflection (doubling, silence e, etc.)
rubrics_metrics.description: Rules about preserving silent e (singe → singeing), doubling final consonant when forming participles or adding endings (commit → committing), and other orthographic matters when forming inflected forms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains when to double consonants and when to drop or preserve final -e; examples and exceptions are included to guide correct spelling.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of 'let' and other special verbs
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Let' before first person expresses entreaty or an ardent resolution (let me die with him; let us go hence). Some verbs habitually take another verb in the infinitive without 'to' (bid, dare, need, see, bear, feel, etc.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guidance on fine differences of mood and required syntax for special verbs; examples illustrate proper usage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Placement of prepositions and pronoun governance
rubrics_metrics.description: The preposition should precede the pronoun it governs; use 'with whom' not 'with who'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples demonstrating correct prepositional governance and advising the pupil on standard placement.
